title: As long as space remains: the vow to stay
hook: vows say 'till death us do part'; Shantideva's promise runs as long as space, and Matthew's Gospel has a neighbor to it
carry: the bodhisattva vow: stay while anyone suffers
tomorrow: a whole poem behind you. which one verse would you keep?

segments.voice: Yesterday: every road, the detours too, for strangers as much as friends. Now Shantideva makes a promise with no end date on it.
screen: `EVERY ROAD.` → `A PROMISE WITH NO END DATE.`

segments.voice: A lease says twelve months. An old wedding service says "till death us do part." A friend at midnight says i'm always here for you, and mostly means it. Every promise to stay comes with a length. Near the end of his poem, Shantideva names his. For as long as space remains, and for as long as living beings remain, may I remain too, to clear away the suffering of the world.
screen: `TWELVE MONTHS. TILL DEATH.` → `EVERY PROMISE HAS A LENGTH.` → `AS LONG AS SPACE.`

segments.voice: So, the question: how long would you stay for someone? Shantideva's answer: as long as anyone needs it. Space doesn't run out, and in his verse, neither do the beings who need help. This is the bodhisattva vow at full size. Not one lifetime of kindness, but staying, life after life, while anyone still suffers. Notice it's said as a wish: may I remain. It's a direction to face, not a schedule to keep. And here a neighbor tradition says something that rhymes with it. At the very end of the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus tells his followers: "lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world." Two promises to stay as long as the world lasts. That's what they share: a love that doesn't plan its exit. And here's the honest difference. In Matthew, Christians hear the risen Christ promising his presence; it's a promise given to them. Shantideva's is a vow taken: someone still on the path, wishing to remain and help across many lives. One is received. One is made. Each means what it means in its own house, and neither has to become the other to be beautiful.
screen: `AS LONG AS ANYONE NEEDS IT.` · `A WISH: MAY I REMAIN.` · `MATTHEW: I AM WITH YOU ALWAY.` · `A PROMISE GIVEN; A VOW TAKEN.` · then, large: `AS LONG AS SPACE REMAINS.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and any scrap of paper. Write Shantideva's promise in your own words, as plainly as you'd text it, short enough to fit on the back of your hand. Then read it back once, slowly, and let it sit.
As long as space remains: Shantideva's vow to keep helping for as long as space and living beings last.

segments.voice: The line to keep: the bodhisattva vow, to stay while anyone suffers, a promise with no exit planned. Forty-nine of fifty.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists and others recite this verse, sometimes at the close of a teaching or with the bodhisattva vow; for Christians, Matthew 28:20 is the closing line of Matthew's Gospel.
